utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Very good afternoon to everybody. Today we don't want to lose any time, so therefore the decision on the admission of the documents has been filed. It will not be read out, just to tell the Defence that in case the Defence is of the opinion that appeal is appropriate, then having reviewed the reasons for the appeal, in principle, the Trial Chamber is prepared to grant a certification. But we shouldn't hesitate any longer. And we should try whatever we can to conclude the hearing of Mr. Sivac today. But let's try and find out whether it's possible or not. So, please, start with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, want to call the case? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sometimes it's better to have for the record, yes, I want to be very brief. Yes, it's better to have the case and the appearances.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And the appearances, for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Nicholas Koumjian, Ann Sutherland, Michael McVicker, with Ruth Karper for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Once again, good afternoon, Your Honours. Branko Lukic assisted by Mr. Danilo Cirkovic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Koumjian, for this reminder. Okay, please start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Lukic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Sivac.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My name is Branko Lukic, and together with Mr. John Ostojic, whom yesterday you had an opportunity to see, I represent Dr. Stakic before this Tribunal as his Defence counsel. Since the two of us speak the same language, our speed can sometimes cause problems. So when I ask a question, would you be so kind and wait a little before you proceed with giving your answer so that the interpreters can have enough time to interpret. In the cross-examination, we have to give references, that is, numbers of pages of previous statements or previous transcripts. Do not be confused with that because this is just for the purposes of the record and pursuant to a request of the Chamber. Are you ready to proceed?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sometimes when I'm waiting, it doesn't mean that I'm not happy with your answer. I'm just waiting for the interpreters to interpret what you have said. I should like to begin with some questions concerning your testimony given yesterday and the day before yesterday. And after that, we will have to try and clear up some other issues concerning a few other documents. So first of all, I would like us to discuss your testimony of Monday, which is the 58th day of the trial. On page 6.559, line 1 and onwards, you mentioned the fact that the chief of the public security service was never a Muslim. Hasan Talundzic was appointed chief of SUP at that time. Are you familiar with Mr. Sead Besic? Does the name ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am. I would like to categorise him as a reserve Muslim. He was married to a Serb woman. He used to work for the State Security Service. And he was part of the political nomenclature at that time. He was a member of the League of Communists, and I do not consider him to be a true Muslim, which is something that he showed as well during the ethnic cleansing of Prijedor. While all residents of Prijedor were being taken to the camps, he was actively working for the State Security Service in Banja Luka. After these events, he was pensioned off.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, is he a Bosniak by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think he is. He declared himself as a Yugoslav, which was a kind of asset or a recommendation which was quite useful for the political functions that he had. He seemed to have been ashamed of his ethnic background.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He said he was part of the political nomenclature of the then League of Communists.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He moved from one office to another within the Prijedor Municipality. I think he served in all of these political offices. He was even at leading positions at various local companies. This is something that it was thought that he deserved, because he was a willing pupil of the gentlemen from the communist party committee. In Prijedor, it was easier to negotiate with any Serb occupying any significant political function than with Sead Besic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, was it not customary for the political officials to move from one office to another? It was not characteristical only for Sead Besic.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to a certain extent, you are -- you are correct. It was necessary for you to be politically suitable at that time and not necessarily competent. As I said, if you were part of the nomenclature and if you were willing to carry out all the decisions and directives issued by the communist party, there should have been no problem for you, as a local politician, to move from one political office to another. Regardless of the fact that such people often had ample opportunity to destroy the local company that they were working at and to mess up things generally speaking, and that is what happened with -- that was the case with Sead Besic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sead Besic, was he ever chief of the Prijedor SUP before Hasan Talundzic?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he had just come from the Energopetrol company, he had worked there previously, and he was the head of the Prijedor SUP for a while, for a brief period of time. And when the national parties came to power, he moved aside and left for Banja Luka, in order to continue his work there for the State Security Service.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I ask that the witness be requested to pause after he hears the question to allow me to hear the translation. I haven't yet had an objection, but if I do have an objection to the question, I have to hear the translation first, and also it gives the interpreters a chance to catch up before he answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Indeed, it would be kind. And I just move forward to requesting the same, it would be kind enough if both of you try not to overlap and to slow down a little bit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the same page, 6.559, you claim that it was not possible for anyone to become a chief of SUP in the Prijedor Municipality without his appointment having previously been approved by the president of the municipality and other authorities and bodies in the local government in Prijedor Municipality. My question in relation to this would be as follows: Was this something that was specific only for Prijedor, or is it your testimony that this was the same case with any other municipality in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was working for the security service, this principle was applied in every municipality in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I don't think I said that it was the president of the municipality who had to issue an approval for the appointment of the security services chief. I think I was referring to the Municipal Assembly. Of course, the Municipal Assembly is always headed by a president. In addition to all other necessary recommendations and approvals, after the multiparty elections, it was necessary for such a person to be a member of one of these parties, and also to be suitable for this type of office. That would have been the main asset, the main recommendation. Whether the individual in question was professionally competent for this type of job, that didn't seem to be very important.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Municipal Assembly, or its president, were they able to issue orders to the chief of SUP?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were required to cooperate closely. I stated previously that, generally speaking, the security situation in the territory of the municipality is within the competence of the chief of this service, who, in turn, was required to report on the security station to the president of the municipality, if they wanted to have the situation and the municipality in general to function adequately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they have --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter can't follow the speakers at this speed. Could the counsel be asked to repeat his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask you again to slow down and not to overlap. But first of all to slow down. I know it seems to be a little bit unnatural when one wants to give an answer, but here it's necessary. Otherwise, we can't understand either the question or the answer, and it's necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell me if the Municipal Assembly and its president could, at the time, issue any order to anyone within the Prijedor SUP?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course they could.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you now tell us whether this was provided for in the law on internal affairs or in the rules of procedure of the State Security Service or the statute of the Prijedor Municipality or any other statutory document, statutory provision?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to admit that I was never very much involved with these procedural and statutory matters. But I know, from previous period of time, while I was still working for the security service, that the chief of the security service was appointed by the republican secretary. But upon a recommendation of the local level, that is, the Municipal Assembly and other relevant organisations. That is, the local committee of the League of Communists, the organisation of war veterans, and some other similar organisations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. I'm not going to dwell on the statutory aspect of this problem. I just want to know whether the Municipal Assembly or its president were able to act or order something which would have not been provided for in any relevant law?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 6.560, you told us the following: "Until Milos Jankovic was appointed --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Page 6560?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Line 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I have a blank page, 6560. It continues after 6559 with 6561.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I think it's at 14.37 or 14.48, somewhere in that range.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't have time here, and I took it from our laptop from our table. So it may cause great problems today if these numbers do not match.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. Therefore it's only fair to ask you to continue. Let's find out if we can work on this basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, can you give me the page number you have which starts on line 11 "my service was one of the most delicate services."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 61. So for now, we have to add only one page.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On line 12 of the page we just indicated, you stated the following: "Up until the time when Milos Jankovic was appointed chief of the security service, there had been a most rigorous control as to the number of employees in terms of their ethnic background." Sir, can you tell us in what year Milos Jankovic was appointed to this office?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was appointed to this office sometime in 1982 or 1983. I cannot remember the exact year. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Just the quotation would be correct "their national background."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] In our country, it's the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I can read only the English version. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, can you tell us whether at that time, from 1982 until 1989 when you left this job, was the League of Communists in power during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but the party was already disintegrating. You know that after Tito's death, it was merely -- it was only a formal organisation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it your testimony that during that period of time, the so-called national key principle was not being respected?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it really depended. Sometimes, in respect of certain offices, it was, and sometimes it wasn't. In my service, there were eight to ten employees, and ethnic background of the employees was always taken into account because of the specificity and the particularity of this job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 6563, you speak about a division of villages. You told us that the railway line or the main road divided the area so that the villages at the foot of Kozara Mount were mostly pro-partisan, whereas the villages on the south side of the railway line were mostly pro-Chetnik. Did you have Serb villages in mind when you spoke about this division, that is, that the Serb villages were divided into pro-partisan and pro-Chetnik villages?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was an imaginary line, of course, something that we learned about in school. We had to listen for about 50 years that the Chetniks never set foot in Maricka, Jelicka, and other villages of the area towards Manjaca. That is, that the area that there were a lot of pro-Chetniks in the area of Manjaca at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any partisans there in the area of Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any partisans in Maricka?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Let me tell you, in the area of Maricka, Jelisca, and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Omarska, there was only one monument to a man who had fought fascists. I think his name was Brane Prokopic, and his monument, that is, the monument dedicated to him, was located in Omarska. A school was called after him there. I think that he was active somewhere in the area of Belgrade or Zemun, not in the area of Omarska and Maricka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there a partisan cemetery in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their Honours should know that in 1944, the communist party and Tito, its leader, issued a decree, an amnesty, so to speak, whereby all Chetniks were pardoned for their sins in the Second World War. Some of them moved over to partisans and fought with them until the end of the war, thereby securing for themselves very decent partisan pensions that they enjoyed until the rest of their lives. And I think that this monument was erected to the memory of these people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know this, or is that what you think?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what I learned in school. I went to high school, and well, I don't know what school you attended.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that Dr. Stakic's grandfather had his name inscribed at Mrakovica as a partisan who was killed?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you something about that which might disappoint you. For many years, I wrote articles about the memorial on Mount Kozara. When this memorial was erected, the names of over 10.000 so-called partisan fighters were engraved there, but among them were Chetniks, who in 1944 were pardoned and who passed over to the partisan side. Those names up there were collected from all the municipalities gravitating toward Banja Luka and Prijedor. Maybe Milomir Stakic's grandfather was a Chetnik for a time, and then in 1944, crossed over to the partisan side. I don't know really what his grandfather's story is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the same sort of amnesty proclaimed for the Ustasha?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 6.568, you speak of an announcement read out over Radio Prijedor, line 14 forward. You say that the announcement was that the SDS had taken over power with the help of the army and the police. Was that actually read out, or was this your conclusion? And was the same announcement published in the next issue of the Kozarski Vjesnik newspaper?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what sort of announcement was published in the Kozarski Vjesnik, but I remember well that after the takeover of power, a lot of announcements were read out and a lot of instructions as to how the population was expected to behave. I don't know which announcement you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about the announcement on the takeover of power.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. You are putting the things together. The sentence on the announcement, I can't find this kind of --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Line 23, 22 and 23.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This is the issue. There, the witness stated that there was a total chaos in the municipality, and that that was the reason why the people from the SDS assisted by the military and the police had carried out a military coup, and that they had taken control of all of the positions and so on. So, it's not related to the announcement as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 6.569, line 9, you say: "The listeners of Radio Prijedor were able to hear the new president of the municipality of Prijedor, Mr. Milomir Stakic, who, in his speech, repeated everything that had already been said in the announcement I mentioned." Was Dr. Stakic interviewed or did he read out the announcement?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, as far as I can remember, Mr. Stakic read out the announcement. But he changed it a little. He mitigated it somewhat, made it more acceptable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If the journalist interviewing him said something different, would he be lying?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you: I didn't hear an interview with Mr. Stakic. This was an announcement he made to the citizens of Prijedor directly. He simply read out the text which had been prepared for him in the Crisis Staff probably. It was probably done by Milenko Rajlic, his right-hand man, who wrote those pamphlets and all the other material that was read out on behalf of the Crisis Staff on Radio Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's why I asked you if the journalist who was in the studio with Dr. Stakic were to say that Dr. Stakic did not read out the announcement, would he be lying.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he would be lying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know about a session of the assembly of the Municipality of Prijedor held on the 16th of May, 1992, on the day when Prijedor was liberated and this was a solemn session?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, and at that time, I was not interested in this because on the 30th of April, there was a takeover of power. And the people who took over power with the help of the army and the police, they had staged a coup. And as far as I was concerned, this event was no longer what it had been before. And this was not only my opinion, but the opinion of all the other non-Serbs who lived in the municipality of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know about a session of the Serbian Assembly of the Municipality of Prijedor held on the 20th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, my only information about these events was from the Kozarski Vjesnik and Radio Prijedor. Let me clarify: As early as March 1992, my cooperation with the Sarajevo television station had been blocked totally. On the airwaves of Radio Sarajevo you could hear only a correspondent from Radio Prijedor who was able to use the radio to send his reports, and there were no opportunities for us to send any film to the television in Sarajevo. The studio in Banja Luka we used to send images to Sarajevo was in the hands of the Serbian party and their supporters, and we were not allowed to use a videolink to send images to Sarajevo. All of a sudden, the studio of Sarajevo Television which was located in Banja Luka became the studio of the Serbian television of Bosanska Krajina. And this happened overnight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a Crisis Staff of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor, and did it exist at the same time as the Serbian Assembly of the Municipality of Prijedor, or did one follow the other?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The assembly of the Municipality of Prijedor had to have a Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your view, they existed in parallel, both the Crisis Staff of the Serbian assembly and the assembly of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. We have to clarify this. You have to make this clear to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will try.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know that in January 1992 -- no, let me go back to 1991, late 1991. Had Dusan Jankovic then been the legally elected police chief in Prijedor and the deputy of Hasan Talundzic, with the help of his collaborators and under the eye of Simo Drljaca, in November, he started establishing a Serbian police force, a Serbian security service. In January 1992, and this was all well-known, although it was supposed to be secret, the Serbian Municipality of Prijedor was established. And in April, I think it was the 14th of April, 1992, the holders of the main positions in the Serbian assembly -- in the Serbian Municipality of Prijedor were appointed. This is really absurd. Dusan Jankovic, Milomir Stakic, they were legally elected. They were legally appointed by the government which was composed of the SDA and the SDS, but at the same time, they worked on establishing parallel Serbian institutions without even concealing the fact. This is absurd. It's nonsensical, that a person should hold a certain post, but do his best to sabotage, to undermine, the institution where they are performing their duties in order, to prepare a takeover of power and everything else that was to follow.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I must go back to the question I put to you. Perhaps it was not sufficiently clear. Do you know whether at the same time the Crisis Staff of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor existed at the same time as the Municipal Assembly or did one come after the other in a time sequence? Do you know this?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the Prijedor SUP after the takeover of power, was there a Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff was set up as soon as power was handed over. The Serbian Crisis Staff, which excluded the others, and all the posts were assigned to Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It seems that again, I was not clear enough. Within the framework of the Prijedor SUP, was a Crisis Staff established?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only within the Prijedor SUP?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was some sort of coordination committee which included people holding posts in the security service. How this committee or staff was established, well, it wasn't a real staff. It was simply to facilitate the coordination of the various police stations that had been set up in 1991 by Dusan Jankovic with the help of his associates who organised the Serbian security service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you all this to make it clearer to you because when you said on page 6.569 that on the 12th of May, 1992, Ranko Mijic told you that he had been issued an order by the Serb authorities and the Crisis Staff to have your equipment taken away, I want to put it to you that the Crisis Staff of the Municipality of Prijedor did not exist before the 22nd of May, 1992. That is why I'm asking you these questions. You may be referring to some other Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's just it. Ranko Mijic didn't tell me which Crisis Staff. He just said: "The Crisis Staff." And in view of the fact that, well, I wasn't there to see whom he had consulted. Whether it was a staff in Banja Luka or somewhere else, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 6.572, line 18, you say that announcements on Radio Prijedor were read out by announcers whose voices you knew, "Senija Dzafic, a Muslim, Jadranka Vejo, unfortunately also a Muslim." Do you consider that the people who remained and worked under the Serbian authorities were Prijedor are traitors?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of them, yes. But only those who while performing their job committed crimes or actively took part in the actions that led to the disappearance of their own people. Sead Besic is one of those who betrayed his own people. He was formerly in the League of Communists in Prijedor. He was in charge of staffing there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Just for clarification, the quotation is to be found on 6.573 in this case. It was correctly quoted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the bottom of page 6.573 and the beginning of page 6.574, you say -- rather, you describe the beginning of the attack on Prijedor, or the liberation of Prijedor, on the 30th of May, 1992. You say that the attackers or the liberators, depending on what view you take, were people of Bosniak and the Croat ethnicity, and you say that initially they were armed only with light infantry weapons. Did this group of people also possess rockets which were allegedly fired on the hotel?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The group led by Slavko Ecimovic had several Zolja rocket launchers among their weapons. And according to the information I have, and what I learned later on, these Zoljas had been bought from Serbs, a certain number of Serb soldiers returning from the battlefields in Croatia. Only a few of these Zoljas were in working order while all the others were out of order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You, of course, have no personal experience of this, but only learned this through hearsay.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard this from people who were part of the group that tried to liberate Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And who survived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 6.575, line 12, you say: "The old town was in flames since the early morning hours." After that day, what condition were the houses in, the buildings, in the old town?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that day?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's say the 31st of May or the 1st of June.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that day, there were no buildings left in the old town. There were only ruins.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In any case, they were not habitable, these ruins?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Let's take it in chronological order, sir. When the town was set on fire, the old town began to burn when the Serb soldiers and police entered it. And I watched from my flat long columns of elderly people, women, children, and men with white armbands moving down the streets led by a person called Adem Music carrying a white flag. He was a man I knew well. They were carrying bundles, and the Serb soldiers were escorting them on both sides. There was even a tank escorting them. These people were led out of the old town, and then the burning, destruction, and looting continued. By these actions, I mean, the burning and the destruction of the old town, all this was under the command of a man called Supic. I know him well. Before that, he was elected president of some sort of Chetnik youth organisation in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. On the same page, line 19, you say that "both mosques were destroyed and set on fire during the initial attack." Are you referring to the same day?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the same day. But it was around noon when Slavko Ecimovic's group and the group of survivors had long left the area of the old town. They went across the Sava, and they went back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the record, you are probably referring to the Sava -- Sana, not the Sava.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise if I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were arrested twice in June. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first time it was on the 10th of June or thereabouts?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were you arrested for the second time?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was sometime around the 20th of June. Again, I'm not sure about the exact date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Around the 20th of June is good enough. Thank you. On both Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. occasions, you were driven away in a police van.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. The first time I was sitting behind the driver and the escort in the glassed-in area, and the second time I was at the back of the van which is completely closed off.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many rows of seats are there in a police van?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. All I remember was that when we were taken in this police van for the second time, there were five of us men. As for the front part, Sifeta Susic and Tesma Elezovic were there, the women who had also been arrested and taken to the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this glassed-in area, how many seats are there? How many people can sit there?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was taken there for the first time, there were four of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it a converted police van or a standard police van?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was a standard paddywagon, or a black Maria, as they used to call it and while I was in service, it was quite active.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the case against Miroslav Kvocka and others, in the Omarska case, on page 4.102, you stated the following: "Together with me" -- I will read out the English version of your testimony so that the interpretation can be appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... In English line 4 and 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the van with me sitting with me at the back side was Omer Kerenovic, Safet Ramadanovic, Ivica Muntijan and myself."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It was the 10th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Line 11 through 14, Defence and Prosecution counsel are discussing which date, and it says 10th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: That's correct, but I don't know if counsel realises that the answer he got in court regarded the 20th of June that Mr. Sivac just testified to.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me which line he is referring to the 20th of June?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Today, I'm sorry, just a few moments ago, your question about how many people were in the van, he was answering regarding the 20th of June, the second arrest, the way I read that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I can clarify it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was together with Mr. Omer Kerenovic, Mr. Safet Ramadanovic, and Mr. Ivica Muntijan that you were taken away. What date was it?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the 10th of June, it was my first arrest, and I said we were sitting behind with respect to the driver and the escort. We were not actually sitting in the back part, the rear part of the police van.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this glassed-in area of the van, there were four of you plus two escorts?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, when we were first taken to the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 6.611, line 23, you said the following: "All orders and everything else happening within the camp Omarska was in the competence of Meakic, and later of Miroslav Kvocka."

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is, again, misrepresentation. I may have inadvertently confused the order of these two commanders in Omarska. First, it should be Miroslav Kvocka, and then Zeljko Meakic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it your testimony still today that Miroslav Kvocka was the first commander of the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is still my testimony.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was also your testimony in the Omarska case?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that this Tribunal has concluded that Miroslav Kvocka had never had this position in the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know, after everything that's happened --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The witness can't comment on the jurisprudence and former discussions of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you, Your Honour. I withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 6.612, line 8, that is, beginning from line 6, when asked whether you had talked with Milos Jankovic about your arrest on the 10th of June, you replied: "I saw him after that, and I asked him who had signed my arrest warrant. He said that it could have been signed by anyone in the SUP. That there was a total chaos there, and that most frequently such orders, such warrants, were written by the Crisis Staff and the people such as Simo Drljaca, Dule Jankovic, even Ranko Mijic. As regards my warrant, or the arrest warrant in respect of my sister, I don't know. I have never been able to find out who it was who signed these two arrest warrants."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This was page 6.617.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] 1-7?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this the same Milos Jankovic with whom you talked and who had sacked you, with whom you had had a verbal conflict, and even a physical conflict in 1989?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. However, despite all this, Milos and I have maintained contact to this date. He talked to me. He did talk to me after all these events, and when I was released from the camp, he told me that whatever had happened in Prijedor was a result of a crazy situation and that there had been a catharsis in the meantime. He said that he had a total different idea of what would happen in Prijedor and that the chaotic situation that prevailed in Prijedor was taken advantage of by certain individuals. He mentioned Simo Drljaca, Dusan Jankovic, Milomir Stakic, and others as individuals who had enriched themselves amidst this chaos and were actually war profiteers, whereas others didn't gain anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you in any of your numerous statements ever mention this detail?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have mentioned it somewhere. I no longer remember. I indeed gave a large number of statements for the media, for the papers. I think that after all, I tried to protect Milos Jankovic. I didn't want him to have any problems with Serbs with whom he was living in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's something missing in the record, so I have to go back, whether you said "maybe I didn't."

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I ever mentioned this for the reasons that I just indicated, not only Milos Jankovic but a number of Serbs who were not supporting the pro-fascist policy of the SDS, for the purposes of their safety and because of the fact that they lived there. Maybe one day, I will write a book with the title: "The Good People in Times of Evil."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that occasion, did Milos Jankovic say what Crisis Staff in particular he was referring to?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was not necessary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 6.6 -- I think -- 18, line 17, you spoke about Mile Mutic. You said that he had a military telephone line installed, that he attended meetings of the Crisis Staff, and that he even personally invited residents of Hambarine, Kozarac, and other parts of Prijedor Municipality which were predominantly Muslim to surrender weapons. And that he also told them that Serb authorities were prepared to guarantee their safety. Was Mile Mutic a member of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mile Mutic was not a member of the Crisis Staff. However, he closely cooperated with them. And everything that was broadcast over his - I have to tell you - his station, Prijedor radio station, had its origins in the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever publish the fact that Mile Mutic was a member of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that I did, but it was just a first impression. It's just that I couldn't understand how come that Mile Mutic was doing what he was doing in 1992 in Prijedor, reading these announcements over the Prijedor radio. So I may have thought that he was doing this because he was a member of the Crisis Staff, whereas he was just the chief of the Prijedor radio station and Kozarski Vjesnik. Later on, I inquired and learned that he was not a member of the Crisis Staff, but he did interpret their views very often.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] I wouldn't know the page number now probably, it's the fourth page from the back of the Monday, 29th of July, 2002, transcript. Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's try to do it this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I think Mr. Lukic is waiting for the page number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This would be 6.630.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's wait what you are quoting. Then I give you the correct number.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Asking for your assistance but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No, no, it's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 6.630, line 24 onwards, you speak about Asmir Crnalic, Vico. You testified about this in the Omarska case as well, and also described it in one of your statements. However, each time, you give a different version. On Monday, you told us that you had seen Asmir Crnalic, that he had suddenly got up without approval of a witness that that he had had a glass or a bottle in his hand, that he was pretending to be drinking water. In relation to this event, in the Kvocka transcript of the 11th of July, 2001, you stated on page 4.098, lines 3 to 4, the following: "Crnalic got the water from the detainees. And he started spitting it out towards the guards." It may seem insignificant at this moment, but can you tell us what happened exactly.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the previous case, I think I already indicated that my statement with respect of this event had erroneously been interpreted. I always wanted it -- my testimony to reflect the fact that Crnalic had taken a glass which contained no water, and that it looked as if he was spitting out water in the direction of the guards. He obviously couldn't do it because he didn't have any water. And that's exactly what the problem was. He was not able to get any water.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Just to make the record clear, Your Honours, I believe the lines quoted by counsel from the Kvocka case were actually part of the question and not the witness's answer. Then the question, counsel was apparently quoting from a statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It seems to be correct. It starts on page 4097, line 24, the question, and then the answer of the witness starts only on page 4.098, line 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] I appreciate any kind of assistance with these numbers. Thank you, once again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you actually see how Asmir Crnalic was killed?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Asmir Crnalic, Vico?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise. Asmir Crnalic.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After he had been taken to the white house, the guards who had escorted him there were on the way back to the administration building. All of a sudden, we heard a command: "Lie down." And then a burst of gunfire, or was it single shots? I don't remember any more. We saw through a glass wall a guard who was standing at his guard post with his rifle pointing towards the white house. We lay down on our stomachs, and it was our assumption -- the assumption which we were able to confirm later on that he had indeed been killed by this guard who always stood guard on this position, on this post.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Vico try to run away?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't see that, nor could we see that. But judging by the position in which his body was at that moment, which was lying outside the white house beneath the window of the first room to the left, and let me tell you, of course it was possible for him to leave the white house, to get out of the white house. But he obviously couldn't run away. There were -- there was a number of guards who were alert all the time. There were actually three rows of guards at all times, and there was also a mine field in between. So it was not possible to escape.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 12th of November, 1994, in the statement that you gave to the officials of this Tribunal, on page bearing the number, last four digits, 7541, in paragraph 1, you said that "Asmir Crnalic was trying to jump out of the window, and that he had managed to jump out of the window, and then the guards shot him." Is this correct, what you stated in your statement?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is this my statement or the transcript from my testimony in the Kvocka case?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I was referring to your statement given on the 12th of November, 1994. Actually, the statement was given from the 12th to the 16th of November, 1994.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was the statement that I gave at the time. As regards any other details --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] On page 31, paragraph 2, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry, this time, I don't have the statement before me, none of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have extra copies for everybody, but probably we are going to introduce these statements later, Your Honour. If you wish --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Of course, it would be of assistance that we, for the record, have the quotations. May the usher please distribute these copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would it be an appropriate time, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did counsel quote from the page number from the B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Later on, I gave the English version as well. It's page 31, paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it's appropriate to have the break right now until 10 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I hope that Your Honours have the statement now. And Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. do you want me to go back and ask this question again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please, do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So it's page 31, the second full paragraph, starts from the line 4 in that paragraph and says: "My friend Asmir Crnalic was lying on the pista. He was a mental patient. He needed some water so stood and demanded water. A couple of guards approached. Asmir was having a nervous attack and he was agitated. A prisoner gave him a small bottle of water, and he began spitting it towards the guards. They took him to the white house. The white house had short walls with large glass area so we could see clearly. Then we heard shouts and shooting. `Vico' (Asmir Crnalic) was trying to jump from the window. He did. He had lost control. He did jump down, and the guards shot him dead. The guards said he was shot trying to escape."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sivac, do you see any difference in the description of this event which you gave in November of 1994 and on Monday?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you, sir: When I recount this event, I sometimes become emotional, perhaps. But I abide by my first statement because in 1994, my memory was fresher, and I remembered more details. I see now that these details are very important to you. The essence is true. Asmir Vico was a sick man. He was taken to the white house. When he tried to escape from the white house to the pista, he was shot. At about 7.00, when the guards changed shift, Kos, Krle and Ckalja were on the pista, but whose shift was until 7.00 and whose shift started from 7.00, I don't know. But in essence, this is quite true. Ckalja asked who the man's name was, and I told him. He wrote it down on a piece of paper, and that was the end of this incident.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is true that we are interested in details here. Please understand that a criminal trial is, in fact, concerned with details.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand you, but you should understand us also. Ten years is a long time. These events happened long ago, and unfortunately people forget these small details which are important in all this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will now talk about the transcript of yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to the Chamber, but on yesterday's transcript, I had to prepare last night, so I have the page numbers starting from 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No problem. We, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] I hope that at least these pages would match.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 3 of yesterday's transcript, that is, Day 59 of the trial, in line 8, you say that there were between five and seven hundred prisoners on the pista. Is this estimate correct, or did you give other figures on other occasions?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is my approximate estimate. And let me repeat that the number of prisoners on the pista often changed radically.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there ever 2.000 prisoners on the pista, and is it possible to fit that number of people on the pista?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me repeat: This is just my opinion. I don't know if I ever said that there were 2.000 prisoners on the pista.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We will come back to this when we go through the book you published.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, I would like to ask the usher to distribute a document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask for the source of this draft.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry. I asked for the source of this unsigned draft.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] I'll try to establish it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Are there any objections from the Office of the Prosecutor to work with an unsigned draft?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Not yet, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then please proceed. "Volenti non fit injuria," the one who volunteers doesn't receive injustice. So please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an objection, too. I have been given the English version. I don't understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: For the record, does the Defence have a B/C/S version?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, we don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Doesn't make much sense to present this document to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As we used to do, we quote it from the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. But I recall your interventions and objections to drafts and unsigned documents. So please proceed, but don't ask the witness to read on the one or the other page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sivac, I do apologise, but I do not have a Bosnian version of this document. The Office of the Prosecutor provided this statement together with the other statements they were kind enough to provide us with. This is an unsigned statement of yours taken on the 30th of March, 1998 when you were interviewed by Mr. Erik Hansen. Do you remember this, sir?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember that you made a statement to the Tribunal in 1998?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't remember. I know that in 1998, I was at the Tribunal, and I was supposed to testify at the Kovacevic trial.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 4 out of seven pages of that statement, in the second paragraph, it says: [In English] "I never saw Kovacevic in Omarska." [Interpretation] Do you remember that you said this?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what Kovacevic is referred to here. Is it Ranko Kovacevic or Mico Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you asked about Ranko Kovacevic or Mico Kovacevic on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know because I don't remember that. I assume they asked me about Ranko Kovacevic because Ranko Kovacevic used to round up the people who were to be taken to the SUP in Prijedor. So the question was probably whether he ever came to the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, but when we work with this draft, chapter 3, it starts: "In my previous statement, I mentioned Mico Kovacevic." And then apparently this Mico Kovacevic is discussed in the following paragraphs. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 3 of your statement, under number 3, that is before the sentence we quoted, it says: [In English] "In my previous statement, I mentioned Mico Kovacevic." [No Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I could just interject, based on Your Honours' comment, as you know this is an unsigned statement that was apparently never read back to the witness. That is part of the purpose of reading back. The order in which things are stated does not necessarily mean that that is the order in which the conversation the witness may have had with the investigator took place. It's to clear up those ambiguities that we read it back, just for Your Honours' to consider in evaluating the probative value of an unsigned statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, but tendered by the OTP apparently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Not tendered by the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It was handed over in preparation of the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: On Your Honours' instructions that we hand over any statement. It's not tendered as evidence at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Quite right, I see the distinction quite clear. But then I may ask the usher for clarification to show the witness page 4 of this document. In the middle of the page, left-hand side, there you find some handwriting. Is this your handwriting? And the same is true on page 5, if you could have a look on page 5.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can see, this is not my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The same is true for this remark, 30th of May, 1992 on the right-hand side?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can clarify. It's my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It's your handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So by mistake, we photocopied from the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it's now the climax of confusion, working with photocopies, not signed, the remarks of the parties, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would ask Your Honour only to ask one more question regarding this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There is number 11 in this document on page 6. And I'll try to read it so the answer can answer this question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "I also mentioned in my previous statement that my old colleague, Zivko Ecim filmed a delegation visiting Omarska on 28th July. I don't know if Kovacevic was also present. I did not see him. We were lined up in front of the houses and the delegation walked around." [Interpretation] Was this the delegation that visited Omarska and, as you said, this happened before the 20th of July?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this is not the same delegation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the Omarska camp visited by one or more delegations?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you: People came to the Omarska camp in some sort of delegations, but I don't know who they were representing there. I don't remember when I made the statement. This is something completely new to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your interview with the OTP investigator Suellen Taylor on the 26th of April, 2002: [In English] "By Taylor, asked how many delegations came to Omarska. The witness was only aware of one." [Interpretation] You have just told us that you knew about more than one delegation.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you: This interview was made by telephone, and the lady who talked to me on the phone called me when I was in my car, and I thought she was interested only in this political delegation that they were talking about, that they talked about the last time, I mean. And there was only one political delegation, and that was the one belonging to the Autonomous Region of Bosanska Krajina led by Alija [as interpreted]. But there were other delegations from Omarska and Prijedor which arrived in the administration building, but I don't know why.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that you know of several political delegations that visited Omarska?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know only of one political delegation which I saw when it arrived, but I know that many informal groups or delegations from Prijedor or from Omarska arrived and visited the camp. In one such delegation from Omarska, there was Mladen Radic, a former policeman from Prijedor, he was at the head of this delegation. And with him were several other people whom I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Radic working at the Omarska camp then?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. That was not Mladjo Radic, Krkan, it was another Radic. They happen to have the same name. Mladjo Radic known as "Krampov" is a different person who has nothing to do with Mladjo Radic, Krkan. He also worked with me in the State Security Service once. I remember there was a group of people, you say they were a delegation, led by a man called Sisarica, who was from Prijedor. And they came to Omarska, and he was wearing a Chetnik uniform and asking for Alija Ganic. We knew he wasn't there in the camp at all. He was looking for him because he wanted to kill him. He held him responsible or co-responsible for the death of his son.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the statement, you said you never saw Kovacevic present in the camp. However, you make mention of the 28th of July as the date of the visit.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not sure I was able to situate the event in time in this manner, if we are talking about the 28th of July. It's possible that I made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the statement that you gave to the officials of the Tribunal on the 12 until the 16th of November, 1994, on page last four digits of the B/C/S version 7543, paragraph 2, English version, page 34, paragraph 1, you indicated that the visit happened on the 28th of July. This statement has been signed.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is possible that I made a mistake with the date. In my first interview in 1994, there were many mistakes, and I complained when I first arrived in the Tribunal. The interpreter was a woman by the name of Alma Qureshi, as far as I remember. And I think that it was only when I actually arrived in the Tribunal that I was able to read the entire statement that I had given. And it was during that reading that I realised that it contained a number of mistakes. I remember clearly one sentence. I was speaking in the third person singular, and it was interpreted as if had been said -- in the first person singular. I was trying to explain to the investigator the difference of Muslims in our country and the Muslims in the eastern part of the world, and I said that we European Muslims did not -- that we were not so observant of certain usual customs, that most of us drank alcohol and ate pork.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: First of all, apparently the Defence makes reference to paragraph 4 of page 34. And I would ask the Defence to read out the entire paragraph you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, Your Honour. I have it marked as the last paragraph. I read it the first. I apologise. And I will read the whole paragraph. "About the 28th of July, we were all taken outside. People from all buildings were assembled outside, and Prcac, Mladic (camp commander) and Tadic, Brk, were there. Brk told us that leaders of the SDA were coming and we were to greet their motorcade with the Serbian salute and sing Serbian songs. We were rehearsed all morning. Then they arrived in five cars with a police troop carrier escort. We were ordered to salute and shout "this is Serbia" and then we had to sing the songs. From the convoy, a former colleague and press men I knew emerged. Zivko Ecim, Rade Mutic, Ostoja Kesar, Slobodan Pesevic, Boro Maric. The politicians and reporters found it very funny that we had been made to sing and salute Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. like this. The politicians included Radislav Brdjanin, Vojo Kupresanin, Dr. Radislav Vukic (Rale Monstrum), of the SDS Banja Luka. From the Prijedor SDS were Simo Miskovic, Milomir Stakic, Srdo Srdic, Simo Drljaca, Major Radmilo Zeljaja, and Milan Andzic. Zivko, my old colleague, filmed all this. Since I knew all these people from my former work, I was very afraid to be recognised. The limousines were Audi and Mercedes. One Audi was one taken from a colleague, friend, Rudi. There was a green Merc taken from a doctor, and a red one confiscated from a doctor in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could put on the record my objection to the previous question, where counsel indicated that the witness had stated that the event took place on the 28th of July. The actual quote from the statement is about the 28th of July. The statement was given over two years later, and I think we all need to take into consideration that a person asked two years later about an event normally would have troubles remembering an exact date when that event took place while in a camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please don't comment on this because I asked already to read out, and it reads now from the transcript "about the 28th of July." But I have one additional question. On the top page of the cover page of this, call it, document, one can read: "Dates of interview, 12 to 16 November, 1994." And what does this 5-26-92 on the page mean? You can read it on all the pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I don't know the answer, but I can speculate. It apparently is a footer which, if you've worked with some common software, it's very common that if you're copying -- I think it's common in these cases for the investigators to take a previous document which already has all of the common information, name, nickname, age, and address, and fill it in for the individual witness. Apparently, someone did not change the footer, although I don't know any footer from the Tribunal would be dated 1992 since the Tribunal wasn't in existence at that time. But apparently it's an error in the footer of the document. That's why it shows up on every page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sometimes 5-25-92. But apparently, this can have no real meaning. Probably as we learned earlier, just an invented date. But I take it that this interview was conducted indeed the 12th to 16th November, 1994. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Yes, Your Honour. That's the information -- of course I wasn't present, but that's the information we have. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Defence may proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sivac, can you tell us today whether you are sure that you saw Mico Kovacevic in the month of July 1992 with a delegation from Banja Luka that visited the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this is what I stated in 1994, then I am sure about that, that that was Mico Kovacevic and that the delegation was composed as I indicated at the time. However, from the transcript I can see that part of my statement had been erroneously interpreted. Here it says an SDA delegation, and not a delegation of the Serbian Autonomous Region.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 17th of February, 1992, did you have a telephone conversation with Mr. Tariq Malik?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible that I did. I often had such telephone conversations. However, these telephone conversations should be placed in a special context. It happened quite often that I had to talk while driving and that at that moment I was not able to concentrate on what I was saying and go on driving the car which carried maybe my children whom I had -- which carried children whom I had picked from school, which is my current occupation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have received only an abridged version of this telephone conversation with Mr. Tariq Malik, and this is the only one we can rely on. On page 1 --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... I have it in English also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We have it before us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You have it, okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the bottom of the page, NS, we have only two kinds of initials, TM, for Tariq Malik, and NS, for Nusret Sivac. Under the last appearance of the NS initials, we read the following: [In English] "So Meakic, he presented some kind of report. Brdjanin, from Prijedor, Srdjo Srdic, Simo Miskovic, Simo Drljaca. I'm sure they were there. Mico Kovacevic was there from what I can remember. (Later said he was not sure). There was a group of people, journalists from Prijedor and Banja Luka." [Interpretation] Therefore, on the 17th of February, 2002, you were not sure whether you had seen Mico Kovacevic in the Omarska camp. Is it not correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, sir, let me tell you that it was an informal conversation with Mr. Tariq Malik, and I'm sure I will try to avoid such conversations in the future. I will insist, if Mr. Tariq Malik has anyone to ask me, anything of any significance with respect to the trials that are conducted here, that this be done under normal circumstances. Once again, let me emphasise that I most frequently had informal conversations with Mr. Tariq Malik over the telephone while I was driving with children sitting behind me, and I was saying things that were in my mind -- on my mind at that moment. And it is quite possible that in those conversations with Tariq Malik I skipped certain things. I just wanted the conversation to be over as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, did you state this to Mr. Tariq Malik?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is possible that I did at the time, under the circumstances that I indicated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the end of page 2 of the same document, next to the initials TM, that is, Tariq Malik, we read the following: [In English] "To four times for you to tell me names of persons from Prijedor who were part of the delegation at Omarska."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry, this is a misleading question. It should be read in the context of the entire interview, and apparently this Tariq -- this Mr. Tariq Malik was not informed about that what you Mr. Lukic, just some minutes before read out.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid I didn't understand Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: "TM, I mentioned three to four times for you to tell me names of persons from Prijedor who were part of the delegation at Omarska, and then continuing, why didn't you mention Stakic before?" And apparently, this is not in line with we saw from the document from 1994 when the witness told us about that what -- close to that incident, he discussed as happened about the 28th of July and mentioning there Dr. Stakic. And in the same interview we have before us, this indeed not helpful interview of an interpreter and Mr. Malik, and we should recall that it's mentioned in the beginning that no interpreter was used, and Mr. Malik communicated with the witness using his very basic knowledge of B/C/S he picked up working for IPTF and the ICTY. Note, not been read back to the witness, first. And then on the second page, on several occasions, he mentioned that during this meeting, apparently "Stakic was definitely there." This has to be read in the context. The Defence may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tariq Malik, didn't he ask you on three or four occasions to give him the names of the people from Prijedor as being members of this delegation?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. It is possible that he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You testified yesterday during the examination-in-chief, on page 8, you spoke about the fact that you were usually given inadequate water at the Omarska camp. "What I want to say is that the water was industrial water, not clean in terms of bacterias." Are you aware of the fact that this water was analysed on a regular basis and that analysis subsequently showed that the water was adequate?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you're not right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: How could the witness possibly be aware of that fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] I just asked if he knows. If he doesn't, he can tell me he doesn't.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Lukic, I closely followed the construction of the Omarska iron ore mine complex ever since the beginning of the construction. It was one of the major mines in Europe, and I visited this mine at least a hundred times. And I am fully aware of the kind of water that we drank there. I know that the water that we drank was used only to wash the construction machines. It was red in colour. It was full of sulphur and all other things that normally should not be in the water. There was a water tank which brought water to the guards every other day from the area of Lamovita as far as I know. This water was drinkable but was used only by the guards and the interrogators in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would like the usher to present to the witness the document S15-2I.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sivac, I'm sorry, but I have to ask you once again to indicate for us on this picture the location of Mujo's room.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mujo's room was on the ground floor in this area here. This is the entrance, and just below Mujo's room, there was a fountain or a water tap. I don't know how to call it, how to describe it to Their Honours. I don't know how interpreters are going to interpret this. But anyway, this is where the taps were, the taps with running water.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the day when this delegation of politicians visited Omarska, you were taken out of Mujo's room where you were staying at the time, and your group was lined up outside the administration building. On this picture, you marked for us the spot where you were. Is this how they made you -- where they made you stay until the departure of the delegation?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Milorad Tadic, Brk, brought these groups of detainees here early in the morning, he kept reshuffling these rows of detainees to make them look as nice as possible. But at any rate, the spot where I was at the time of the visit of this delegation was to the left of the fountain, close to the detainees who were lined up outside the garage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So as we look at the picture, it would be closer to the right angle of the administration building.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, more or less here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far could you move?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I came there, no, we couldn't move. But during the morning when Tadic was trying to reshuffle all these people, we did move. He tried to have all of the rows full of detainees so that there were no empty places.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the visit was over, were you immediately returned to the room?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I already stated that I don't know when the -- I didn't know when the visit was over. But after the delegation had passed along this road with Radislav Brdjanin and others going towards the administration building, and when this group with Simo Miskovic and Srdjo Srdic after a brief conversation with Dedo Crnalic who had come up to them to talk to them but they refused to talked to him, we saw immediately Milomir Stakic and Milan Andzic following them. And they turned off behind the garage. After that, we were taken back to the room. But I don't know when it was that the visit actually ended.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How was it possible for you to see the line of people in front of the white house from that vantage point?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the morning hours, when Milorad Tadic, Brk, was lining people up, moving them to the left and to the right, it was possible for us to see that the detainees were also lined up outside the white house which was very strange.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 46, you speak about Zlatan Besirevic. And in line 17, you describe your conversation with him. After his request for transfer to Trnopolje had been refused. You stated the following: [In English] "We asked him why he wasn't being transferred to Trnopolje, he said: `my name was taken off the list, removed from the list in the Crisis Staff.'" [Interpretation] Did you know Zlatan Besirevic well?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew him very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
