utterances.text: Did you ever mention this event in any of your previous statements or in your book?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember. I don't even remember what I wrote about it in my book.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 49, line 19, you state the following: [In English] "When we arrived in Trnopolje camp, it was surrounded with wire fencing." [Interpretation] I should like to know whether this fence could be seen or should have been seen by other detainees in Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the fence was in place until the second day of our arrival, and that is until the 8th or the 9th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the entire Trnopolje camp fenced off, from all sides?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. There was only one passage, one opening, facing the railway lines. And a house which had a well in the front yard. And some of the guards allowed us to go to that well to fetch water for ourselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You then go on to say, on page 52, or rather 51, line 25, you mention Rade Mutic. On the following page, Zivko Ecimovic.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ecim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Zivko Ecim, then. And you describe a situation where they offered you some help in order to get out of Trnopolje. You say: [In English] "They looked at me and they said: `Well, Omarska could not be helped. The release papers for someone to leave Omarska would have had to be signed by someone from the Crisis Staff directly, or by Radmilo Zeljaja, the commander of the 43rd Motorised Brigade.'" [Interpretation] The first thing I would like to ask you is, did you ever mention this before in any of your statements or your book?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know whether I did or not. But I do know it happened because Rade Mutic then told me about an incident where Ratib Seferovic was taken out of Omarska in this way. He was a former employee and director of the commercial centre of Kozarski Vjesnik. But he had to write his biography, and with the help of his CV, and with the people from Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the Crisis Staff, he was released from the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Radmilo Zeljaja was a soldier, was he not?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the commander of the 343rd Motorised Brigade which was later given another number, and it consisted mostly of men from Prijedor of Serbian nationality who in 1991 took an active part in the war in Croatia in the areas of Lipik and Pakrac. After the cease-fire was signed in Croatia, it arrived in Prijedor waiting for the political decision to start their conquest and ethnic cleansing of Prijedor Municipality. Radmilo Zeljaja and his 43rd Motorised Brigade burnt down Kozarac, a town that was 700 years old. And instead of the sign saying "Kozarac," some of his soldiers put up a sign calling the place, "Radmilovo" and this was in the Cyrillic alphabet. They named the town after their commander, Radmilo Zeljaja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the role of the army in the running of the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the chain of command was. I'm not familiar with that. But as a prisoner, I had the impression that they didn't have any business connections with the camp. In the Omarska camp, as well as Trnopolje and Keraterm, there were no soldiers, and that's why I think that the army did not have any authority over these camps and that they were run by the civilian authorities of Prijedor Municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you take seriously Zivko Ecimovic?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ecim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ecim, and Rade Mutic when they said that Radmilo Zeljaja could get you released from Omarska?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Radmilo Zeljaja had a great deal of influence on the politicians, on the political scene in Prijedor at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that his signature was sufficient to get people released from Omarska?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what Rade Mutic told me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see a document allowing someone to leave Omarska?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you: Before I went to Omarska, a small group of people who had been detained in the Omarska camp were questioned and then released. This group numbered about 20 or 30 people. But these same people who were released from Omarska were arrested again and taken to the Keraterm camp. After this, no one was ever released from the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you about something you mentioned just now. Who ran the Trnopolje camp? Was it the police or the army?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Trnopolje camp was run by Slobodan Kuruzovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he a policeman?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Slobodan Kuruzovic was a captain, maybe he was promoted to a higher rank in Croatia, and his deputy was Slavko Puhalic, also known as Ture Mesar, from Prijedor who was a reserve policeman. In the office in Trnopolje, I'm referring to the office of the Serbian Red Cross, which was set up in Trnopolje, Pero Curguz often spent some time there. He was a teacher from Ljubija, and he was also wearing a police uniform. He coordinated the work of the Serbian Red Cross which was just across the road from the Trnopolje camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see a document signed by Mr. Kuruzovic allowing someone to be released from Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I received a document like that. On one side, it was signed by him. On the other side, by Pero Curguz. But these certificates, well, you could get hold of them in various ways, and I spoke of that during my evidence in chief.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Prosecution showed you yesterday a document from which it is evident that the demolition of certain buildings was ordered by the executive committee of the municipal Prijedor assembly. On page 54 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May the usher please present this document, 243B, to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it evident from this document that at the time it was issued there was an Executive Board of the Prijedor Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw this document for the first time yesterday. And yes, it does say here "executive committee" or "board."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you still maintain that it is the Crisis Staff of the municipality that is responsible for the demolition of these buildings?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received information from someone who is employed on this, doing this, two years after these actions were committed, and I trust this person. He informed me that these lists were drawn up retroactively.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long after these events, two years?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. He didn't tell me the date, but approximately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does this mean that the documentation that has to do with this area is not reliable?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that most of the documents in connection with this were either forged or removed somewhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us the source of this information?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I can't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. When you spoke of the group of men who tried to demolish the remains of the Catholic church, what was left of it, can you tell us whether the bell tower was leaning over at the time?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are right. And I don't know whether I called it a bell tower or a spire. But it's interesting to note that it didn't topple over, it just leaned over a little, and then several days later a group of architects from Prijedor who, instead of building up the town, demolished it with lists similar to this one, they tried to topple the bell tower and then used heavy machinery to remove the rubble. This group was led by Dusan Miljus, a civil engineer from the Ljubija mine, who was wearing a leather jacket and carrying a big scorpion pistol at his belt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Leaving aside the vandalism that led to the destruction of the church, was the bell tower dangerous at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you: It wasn't because all the surrounding family houses which were close to the Catholic church and the building of the theatre in Prijedor which used to be one of the most beautiful buildings in the Former Yugoslavia were severely damaged in the explosion in which the Catholic church in Prijedor was demolished. And the people in the houses surrounding it no longer lived in those houses. They couldn't live there because there was no glass in any of the windows, no window panes, no roof tiles, no roofs, and they had to find accommodation elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it a threat to passersby?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Your Honour, this an appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The trial stays adjourned until 6.00 sharp. May I ask all the participants to inform us on the updates from Banja Luka in the -- during the last break I learned that the witness could possibly be there at 9.30. But this should be confirmed precisely at 7.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I could give you also an update on the progress on the video which is not good news because today our computer system has been down completely, or almost completely. We've -- I identified 15 minutes of the tape that I think should be translated. We have a transcript now of about 8 or 9 minutes. Maybe by the end of today, we'll have a complete transcript in B/C/S. It's possible that we could play it and get the translation from the booths, but we will not have the translation, but we will have a transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think we have to wait, indeed, until it's 7.00 sharp, and only then we know what will happen tomorrow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Just to inform the parties that we indeed have to speed up because I learned this moment from Banja Luka the witness is there, and the videolink is established, and we can start tomorrow. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, I will ask you something specific now. Apart from the municipal Crisis Staff, was there a Crisis Staff of the public security station in Prijedor chaired by Simo Drljaca, the chief of the public security station, then Milutin Cadjo, his deputy, Dusan Jankovic, the commander of the public security station, Marko Djenadija, the commander of the traffic police, Dane Bajic, the commander of the Ljubija public security station, and Bosko Petrovic, retired employee of the SUP?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how I defined this group in my earlier statements. But in the security service, this group did exist, and they called themselves "Kolegi" or something of the sort. And they were in charge of the security service with the Prijedor police station and the branch police stations. They coordinated the work in the field. In one of my statements I may have called them a sort of "staff" of the security service, but this group was active in 1992, and it coordinated, as I said, the work of the branch police stations and the central police station in Prijedor, and the other segments of the security service.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] I will ask the usher to distribute a document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sivac, you have before you a statement we received from the Office of the Prosecutor which you made to a commission of UN experts working on the Prijedor project as part of the German participation in this commission. In one of your statements, you said that you remembered making a statement to a German judge. Could it be this statement, if you remember, and if you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I haven't looked at it in detail, but it could be this statement. I'm just looking at it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps we can begin, and you will remember if you spoke of topics I would like to put questions about. In the B/C/S version, there are no printed numbers, just numbers added by the OTP. So could you please look at the page bearing number 7292, and it's the third paragraph in the English version. In B/C/S, it's the last paragraph. In the English version, it's on page 3. It says here: "The Crisis Staffs first appeared in February 1992. The most important members of the Crisis Staffs at that time were the following..." And then it goes on on the next page of B/C/S, Zivko Knezevic, a retired police commander who died later during the war. Bosko Petrovic, secretary of the league of communists, the old communist party in Prijedor. Milutin Cadjo, a retired policeman. Slobodan Kuruzovic, a primary school teacher and later director of that school. Vaso Skodric, another retired policeman from the SUP of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Milan Dragojevic, a butcher and president of the SDS in Urije. Ranko Curcija, a professional driving instructor, and also president of the Radical Chetnik Party. Savan Runjo, a teacher of all people's defence. The so-called ONO and DSZ classes, and finally Miodrag Grubljejic, owner of a private transportation company. Can you tell us what kind of Crisis Staff this was?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were men who helped Dusan Jankovic and Simo Drljaca to establish parallel Serbian police stations at the time, and it says here, by mistake, that I said they were Crisis Staffs. In fact, these were people who actively participated in setting up Serbian police stations together with Dule Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the page which in B/C/S has the last four digits 7299, English version page 5, paragraph 2, you say: "In addition, in answer to questions about the role played by Ostoja Marjanovic, Jovan Vukova, probably Vukoja, and Ranko Travar, I wish to say that it is correct that these three men were also members of the Crisis Staff, but they are less important than the others whose names I have provided in my list." Were you referring to something else here or the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ostoja Marjanovic, as the director of the biggest company in Prijedor, the Ljubija mines, was not formally a member of the Crisis Staff, but he was often present at sessions of the Crisis Staff, and so was Jovan Vukoja. They received instructions from the Crisis Staff which were important for their companies, and they were probably the men through whom the Crisis Staff set up the camps. The camp in Omarska could not have been established had Ostoja Marjanovic not been present at the sessions and had he not actively participated in them. Let me repeat: In my testimony in chief, I said that in the time from the takeover of power by the military coup of the Serbian Democratic Party, it was not important whether someone had a membership card of the Serbian Democratic Party or not. What was important was that all Serbs worked in a concerted way on having the demographic composition of the municipality changed and on making Prijedor and the Prijedor Municipality a part of the Autonomous Region of Banja Luka, to have it annexed to that so-called autonomous region.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question today, however, is whether you say that Ostoja Marjanovic and Jovan Vukoja were not members of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that they were not formally members of the Crisis Staff, but that very often they attended sessions of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we therefore consider them to be members of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, not necessarily as members of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page bearing number 7301 in the upper corner, paragraph 2, or page 7, paragraph 1 of the English version --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Before we turn to this part, may I ask the parties, immediately before the paragraph you just read out on page 5, it says: "I have listed the key people in the power takeover in detail in an overview which I have attached to my statement." I can't see any such attachment. Is it available? And in addition, I take the liberty to add, when you started your line of questions on this document, you mentioned, quoting from the top of my head, that this would be a witness statement before a judge. Apparently, it is not because nothing is mentioned on the presence of a judge in this statement we have before us in the German version, and in addition, it's not signed at all. And even no paraphs [phoen] are at the bottom line of the pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Your Honour, we just got a statement from the witness recognising this statement as his own. And in B/C/S, it doesn't say "attachment; it says "list whose names I mentioned on the list," and we have that list read previously on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Both in English and in German, it reads "list attached to the statement" and in German, it reads, sorry for the interpreters, but it's the same: "In an overview I attach to my statement."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We don't have that attachment. So if the Prosecution has one, we will gladly receive it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: The copy I have before me, the German version ends with the ERN number 00286394, with the last paragraph speaking about Dr. Sadikovic. And I have no further attachment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I'm afraid it's only an extract from a police document following the signature 2 ARP248-94 until 5. It's indeed extremely difficult for the parties and us to work with this deluge of paperwork and to compare it and to identify inconsistencies. But please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We were facing the same problem these days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, in paragraph 2, on page 7301, you say: "The people from Kozarac did not accede to the demands from Prijedor and Banja Luka, and the negotiations were not successful. Instead, they organised, partly with their own weapons bought from Serb sources, a kind of defence patrol." Where did you get this information from?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean? It was broadcast over the Prijedor radio or published in Kozarski Vjesnik. In my statement, when I was referring to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. these events, the statement which was taken from me by one or two police officers in the town where I used to live -- do you wish me to add anything? I mean, I would like to add something to my answer. Your Honours, in Prijedor, after the takeover, a strange situation occurred as regards the security service. The town of Prijedor was already under the control of the SDS and Serb authorities. However, Kozarac, a small enclave on the road to Banja Luka, which was 97 per cent Bosniak/Muslim, had a police station which previously, in normal times, had been under the authority of the security service in Prijedor and the police station in Prijedor. However, after the takeover, the Serb Democratic Party no longer had control over this police station which, therefore, became separate from its central office, the police station in Prijedor. They did not recognise the fact that the Serbs in Prijedor had carried out a military coup, that they had taken over power and disarmed all police officers of Muslim and Croat ethnic background. They tried to organise themselves and took over all the relevant competencies in the town of Kozarac until the final capture of Kozarac by the Serb military and police. Until that time, they had operated autonomously. During the takeover of Kozarac, the Serb military and police killed the majority of employees of the police station in Kozarac. A small number of them were taken to the Omarska and Keraterm camps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 7302, paragraph 1, from line 3 onwards, English version, page 7, paragraph 1, you stated the following: "It was said that over 5.000 men participated in the attack including Seselj men, Arkan's men, and White Eagles. In my opinion, Arkan's men and the White Eagles are two distinct paramilitary groups. The leader of the White Eagles was a Serb whose named was Jovic. The unit were stationed on Mount Benkovac on the grounds of a youth hostel. The commander of all of the military units in this attack, including the paramilitary troops, was Radmilo Zeljaja. He personally spoke on Prijedor radio and ordered the people in Kozarac to surrender their weapons within 24 hours and to put up Serb national emblems." My question in relation to this is whether you yourself heard Radmilo Zeljaja say this over the Prijedor radio?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. On the 24th of May, while the ethnic cleansing of Hambarine was still going on, we heard the voice of Radmilo Zeljaja, of the mad Radmilo Zeljaja as he was introduced by the speaker, who read a very brief ultimatum ordering the residents of Kozarac that the deadline has been moved and that if they did not surrender their weapons until noon the next day, that the Kozarac would be razed to the ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have finished with this statement. Just one other matter: We mentioned Vukoja, Jovan Vukoja. Do you know what his occupation was? Do you know what he did?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a social worker. He worked at the social welfare office in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You worked at the security service. Yesterday you mentioned something which I don't think came out very clearly, and I would like to revisit it today. It concerns the seat of this service. Was it in Prijedor? That is, was the headquarters in Prijedor for the municipality of Bosanska Dubica, Prijedor, Sanski Most, and Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What particular service do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It says here the chief of my department of the security service and mention is made of Stojan Panic.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're taking me back to 20 years earlier. I thought that our main subject was Prijedor in the 1990s.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's why I said the matter remained unclear.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stojan Panic was the chief of security service until sometime late 1980s. I have to emphasise once again to Their Honours the fact that in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the structure of the security service was often changed in Bosnia and Herzegovina. It all depended on who was to be a appointed chief of the security service. Whoever took up office was trying to reorganise the service in their own way. While I was employed there, we changed our official title several times, depending on who the superior was. For a while, we were the regional secretariat for internal affairs. Then the name changed to the municipal secretariat for internal affairs. Then we were sometimes called Security Services Centre. Then the police administration. As I said, it all depended on which politician was to be appointed republican secretary for internal affairs in Sarajevo. Let me answer your question directly, when Stojan Panic was the chief of security service, we were for a while municipal secretariat for internal affairs. And just before he retired, we became intermunicipal secretariat for internal affairs. And as part of this intermunicipal secretariat for internal affairs, there were also municipal secretariats for internal affairs for the municipalities of Sanski Most, Bosanski Novi, and Bosanska Dubica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this explanation.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I said we had finished with the statement, but I would like to go back to page 7302. I'm sorry. Paragraph 3; English version, on page 8, paragraph 3. Here you speak about the refugees in the Mladost Hall and how you went there looking for friends and relatives. You go on to say: "All the men that Serbs considered in any way fit for military service were taken to Keraterm." And then, further down: "Even the Serbs didn't know what to do with so many people and were somehow confused about it. By the second day, buses came to Prijedor and transported women and children from the sports hall to Trnopolje where in the meantime, a camp had also been set up. Some refugees who had relatives in the Muslim neighbourhood of Puharska in Prijedor were allowed to join up with their families." Can you tell us if this was done in order, or was the situation chaotic?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation was chaotic. On that day when Kozarac came under an artillery attack, when they started destroying property in Kozarac town, huge columns of women and children, very few men, were arriving to the sports hall in Prijedor. As I said, the situation was chaotic. Women were crying and screaming. In the process, some of these people had lost their children, their mothers, so they were calling out to each other and looking for each other. However, everybody was confused. No one had, until that point in time, seen columns of refugees. People didn't know what it meant. So all of a sudden, you had this huge column of refugees pouring into the city. And no one knew what to do with them. That same day, as these refugees kept arriving, an intervention platoon appeared some time later. I'm referring to the intervention platoon of the Prijedor police station which was led by Dado Mrdja, Zoran Babic and others. This intervention platoon, that is, its members, started separating women and children and abusing them. Some time later that day, buses arrived, and they ordered these women and children to board these buses. And it was then that they said that they should be taken to Trnopolje. Members of the intervention platoon were very rude, and they did not allow us from Prijedor who had heard about this situation and who had attempted to find relatives or friends in the column of these refugees to approach them. However, several families that had been encircled somehow managed to get out. And later, I heard that they had found accommodation somewhere in the Puharska neighbourhood. When the Trnopolje camp was filled up, the Prijedor authorities allowed for a portion of refugees who were still pouring in to find accommodation in the area of Puharska and stay there with their friends or relatives in order to keep them under some kind of control there. However, several days later, they organised convoys for these people in order to displace them and expel them from Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we briefly go back to 1991, July and August 1991, the time of the withdrawal of the JNA from Croatia and the deployment of the light and heavy artillery on the surrounding mountains. What did the president of the SDA attempt to do at the time? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, in 1991, that is, in late 1991, when the cease-fire agreement was signed in Croatia, and when the war stopped there, large military convoys started coming into the area of Prijedor and Bosnian Krajina. I made several programmes, several coverages of these events, together with some other colleagues. After the withdrawal of the army from Slovenia in these huge military columns, the area of Banja Luka suddenly became the largest military barracks in Europe. A huge arsenal of weapons could be found in the area, the weapons that were in the hands of Serbs. They had huge rocket launchers, the so-called Luna systems, at their disposal. At the sports airfield in Prijedor, several tank units were billeted. And if I may reiterate, the entire area of Prijedor and Banja Luka saw the largest concentration of the remnants of the former Yugoslav People's Army and its weapons. But let me give you a specific answer to your question, Mr. Lukic. It is true that one day, somewhere in the Prijedor neighbourhood of Urije, Dr. Mirza Mujadzic, with his associates, revolted with these movements of military units walking around the town of Prijedor, attempted to obstruct the passage of one of such columns. An incident occurred as a result of that, but this incident was very quickly taken care of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the takeover of power on the 30th of April, 1992, did people try to leave Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did. In Prijedor, there was an agency in the old hotel. It was a tourist agency. And the -- there was a Serb. His last name was Plemic, who was in charge there. And he made use of his Serbian ethnicity, in collaboration with others in Banja Luka, to organise transport by buses as far as Banja Luka, and from there, with a plane which the Serb army had taken from the famous Croatian emigrant Kikas, who tried to bring a load of weapons in by that plane. And the plane was overtaken by Serbian pilots and forced to land at Banja Luka airport, and then confiscated while he was put in prison. This plane was now used to carry out ethnic cleansing. Every day, a lot of money was paid by people who had it and who wanted to leave Prijedor. They were able to travel from Banja Luka to Prijedor by that plane.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Serbs also leave by that plane?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Serbs did not leave by that plane except, perhaps, for a few exceptional cases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 30th of May, 1992, you had a car stolen or confiscated?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which car are you referring to, the official television car or my car, my personal, private car?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Ford Escort.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was my private car.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was confiscated on the 30th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, while the attack on Prijedor was still going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say this was done by a group led by Zoran Karlica?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, my private car, my Ford, was parked in the garage which I had rented long before that and which was located in Partizanska Street. You probably know where that street is in Prijedor. And on that day, the heaviest fighting between Slavko Ecimovic's group and the soldiers of the Serbian army was taking place there. This garage was below Salih Ejupovic's house. He was a relative of mine. And some time before this, he had left to join his family in (redacted). The house - let me say right away - is right next to the Obala restaurant in Partizanska Street where the heaviest fighting was going on between Slavko Ecimovic's group and the Serbian soldiers, army, led by Zoran Karlica. And later on, I learned that all these houses were destroyed in this fighting. They were set on fire. I tried to find out what had happened to my car, and I heard from neighbours who lived in that street that before Salih Ejupovic's house was set on fire, the Serbian soldiers had used a tank to pull my car out using a chain tied to the tank and they had driven my car off somewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask the registry to redact from page 62, line 25, the country, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Zoran Karlica participate in this personally, if you know?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My information was that Zoran Karlica's men had done this. I don't know whether before this Zoran Karlica, either before or after, he was seriously wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he died of his wounds in hospital?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You went to the SUP to ask about the car? Who did you go with? Was it your kum, Armin Basic?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible. I don't remember now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever get your car back?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. In Prijedor, there was a big shortage of petrol, and Serbian soldiers only confiscated cars that used diesel fuel and oil. And my car was left on the street in the town. So I managed to get my car back with the help of connections in the security service.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Your Honour, I would now switch to another topic, and I think that we need at least an hour, hour and a half tomorrow after. Because I don't think that this videolink would take long, both in direct and in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Indeed, we can't afford to waste one minute only doing the remaining time before the court recess. And may I ask the witness, you are prepared to assist us also tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And could you please be so kind and understand that we have to interrupt the cross-examination for the purposes of a videolink tomorrow. This videolink can be established only within a certain timeframe, time window. And therefore, during this time, we can't continue with your testimony. But later during the day, we will continue with the cross-examination and probably some other questions or, if possible, clips from the video provided by the OTP. I was just informed that indeed, not only the witness is there, but also the videolink will be ready for 10.00. Nevertheless, we have to continue at 9.00 sharp, Courtroom I. Then we have the videolink, and let's wait and see what time, in fact, we need. Please understand that I do not rely on time estimates in this case. So therefore, the trial stays adjourned until tomorrow, 9.00, Courtroom I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
